title: Teaching on Purpose #3
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck opens a weekly series on teacher decision-making by arguing that what separates one teacher's technique from another's is situational purpose, not the technique itself. Chiltern Learning Trust frames everything teachers do through six purposes, and this issue takes the first, securing, maintaining and regaining attention, through Lemov's SLANT routine as used by an assistant headteacher. The piece walks through when SLANT suits a routine whole-class reset, such as a '3,2,1 SLANT' countdown while scanning the room. It then shows how the technique can be adapted by narrating the positive for slow-settling classes, and when it is unnecessary because students are already attentive. The move is to treat classroom routines as tools matched to a moment rather than fixed scripts, which makes it a classroom-management piece about teacher judgement.
points: Technique choice is driven by the teacher's purpose in the specific moment, so the same broad purpose can produce very different-looking moves.
A '3,2,1 SLANT' countdown works because it gives students time to finish what they are doing while signalling that the teacher expects full attention.
Narrating the positive between the numbers lets reluctant students opt in without being called out early in the lesson.
A full attention reset is overkill when students are already working attentively; a quick 'pens down, eyes on me' is enough.
No routine is a silver bullet, because teaching is not a routine system and teachers must be ready to adapt or reject techniques.
quotes: I think the answer is purpose. By ‘purpose’ I mean the thing the teacher is trying to achieve, but crucially, in the context of that very moment.

SLANT (Lemov, 2009) stands for Sit up, Listen, Answer questions, Nod and Track the speaker. Teachers use it as a means of securing and maintaining student attention, either on them or on another student who happens to be speaking.

To signal that the expectation has shifted to all students attending to the teacher, who is ready to start teaching, the teacher might say ‘3,2,1 SLANT’ and in between each number, might scan the room to show students that they are actively expecting to see everyone beginning to attend to them.

In these instances, narrating the positive in between each number during the countdown, both reinforces what is expected and sets a positive tone that allows those more reluctant students to choose the expected behaviour.

In this case, returning to the front of the room and issuing a simple instruction like ‘pens down, eyes on me, thank you’ might suffice. If students are already in an attentive state, as with this example, the teacher is simply shifting the focus of their attention and so a full reset (like using SLANT) might be unnecessary.

SLANT is a valuable technique and when used at the right time, for the right reason, it can be super powerful. But like all techniques, it isn’t a silver bullet because teaching isn’t a routine system.
